commands.name: pg_stat_activity
commands.summary: One row per server process: who is running what
commands.description: System view with each connection's user, application, state, current query and wait event.

flags.description: What the backend waits for (Lock, IO, Client…).

examples.title: Running queries
examples.scenario: List PID, user and query of every active backend.
examples.command: SELECT pid, usename, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active';
examples.output:
pid  | usename |                 query
------+---------+---------------------------------------
 4242 | report  | SELECT * FROM events WHERE payload ~ 'x'
 4310 | app     | UPDATE orders SET status = $1 WHERE id = $2

output_notes.meaning: Regex filter over a large table: likely a full scan.
output_notes.anomaly: Long-running ad-hoc queries from reporting roles.

examples.title: Queries running longer than 5 minutes
examples.scenario: Find active queries running for more than 5 minutes.
examples.command:

output_notes.meaning: How long the query has been running.

----------------------

commands.name: pg_blocking_pids
commands.description: pg_blocking_pids(pid) returns the PIDs blocking a backend; combined with pg_stat_activity it shows lock chains.

examples.title: Blocked sessions and their blockers
examples.scenario: List every waiting backend with the PIDs that block it.
examples.command:
SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by, query
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;
examples.output:
pid  | blocked_by |                 query
------+------------+-------------------------------------
 4501 | {4377}     | ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text
 4502 | {4501}     | SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 10

output_notes.meaning: PID holding the lock this session waits for.
output_notes.anomaly: A chain: one idle transaction blocks a migration, which blocks every reader.

commands.name: EXPLAIN ANALYZE
commands.summary: Show and measure a query plan
commands.description: EXPLAIN prints the planner's chosen plan; ANALYZE executes the query and adds real timings and row counts.

flags.description: Run the query and report actual time and rows.
Show shared buffer hits and reads.

examples.title: Measure a slow query
examples.scenario: See the real plan and timing of the lookup of customer 42's orders.
examples.command: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
examples.output:
Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..18334.00 rows=96 width=64) (actual time=0.031..92.114 rows=104 loops=1)
  Filter: (customer_id = 42)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 999896
Execution Time: 92.201 ms

output_notes.anomaly: On a large table with a selective filter: missing index.
Huge: an index on the filter column would help.

examples.title: Plan without running
examples.scenario: Show the plan of a DELETE without executing it.
examples.command: EXPLAIN DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < now();
examples.output:
Delete on sessions  (cost=0.00..4313.00 rows=0 width=0)
  ->  Seq Scan on sessions  (cost=0.00..4313.00 rows=120000 width=6)
        Filter: (expires_at < now())

output_notes.normal: Close to what you expect to delete.
output_notes.anomaly: Far larger: the filter is wrong or stats are stale.

commands.name: VACUUM
commands.summary: Reclaim dead rows and refresh statistics
commands.description: Marks space of dead tuples reusable and, with ANALYZE, updates planner statistics. Autovacuum normally does this automatically.

flags.description: Rewrite the table to return space to the OS (exclusive lock).

examples.title: Vacuum and analyze one table
examples.scenario: After a large delete on orders, vacuum it and refresh its statistics.
examples.output:
INFO:  vacuuming "appdb.public.orders"
INFO:  finished vacuuming "appdb.public.orders": index scans: 1
tuples: 412004 removed, 1000210 remain, 0 are dead but not yet removable
VACUUM

output_notes.meaning: Dead tuples whose space is now reusable.

output_notes.token: 0 are dead but not yet removable
output_notes.meaning: Dead rows still visible to an old transaction.
output_notes.anomaly: Large numbers: a long transaction blocks cleanup.

examples.title: Tables with most dead rows
examples.scenario: Which tables have the most dead tuples and when were they last autovacuumed?
examples.command:
SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC LIMIT 5;

output_notes.anomaly: Millions with an old last_autovacuum: autovacuum cannot keep up.

procedures.title: Triage a database that is slow for everyone
procedures.context: All requests touching the database became slow a few minutes ago.
procedures.goal: Find long queries or lock waits and relieve the pressure.

steps.command: SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state;

output_notes.anomaly: Dozens: something blocks or overloads the server.

steps.interpretation: 63 active sessions is far above normal.

steps.command:
SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS age, query FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active' ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 5;
steps.interpretation: A 31-minute bulk UPDATE is the oldest query.

steps.command:
SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;
steps.interpretation: Sessions wait on 4242: it holds the locks.

steps.command: SELECT pg_cancel_backend(4242);
steps.interpretation: Escalate to pg_terminate_backend only if cancel does not help.

use_cases.title: Lock pile-up
use_cases.situation: One long transaction blocks dozens of updates.

procedures.title: Find and fix a missing index
procedures.context: The orders page takes seconds to load for some customers.
procedures.goal: Confirm a sequential scan and add an index without downtime.

steps.command: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
steps.interpretation: Seq Scan with many rows removed by filter.
steps.output:
Seq Scan on orders (actual time=0.03..92.11 rows=104)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 999896

steps.command: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer ON orders (customer_id);
steps.interpretation: Built online; writes continued during the build.

steps.command: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
steps.output: Index Scan using idx_orders_customer on orders ... Execution Time: 0.180 ms
steps.interpretation: Index scan in under a millisecond: the fix worked.

use_cases.title: Slow customer page
use_cases.situation: Support reports slow order history for large customers.

procedures.title: Back up and prove the restore works
procedures.context: Monthly check that backups of appdb are restorable.
procedures.goal: Dump, restore into a scratch database and compare row counts.

steps.command: pg_dump -U app -Fc -f appdb.dump appdb
steps.interpretation: pg_dump is silent on success.

steps.command: createdb -U app appdb_restore
steps.interpretation: Empty database ready for the restore.

steps.command: pg_restore -U app -j 4 -d appdb_restore appdb.dump
steps.interpretation: Silent restore; errors would print and the exit code would be non-zero.

steps.command: psql -U app -d appdb_restore -c "SELECT count(*) FROM orders;"
steps.interpretation: Row count matches production: the backup is usable.

use_cases.title: Audit requirement
use_cases.situation: Prove backups are tested regularly.

procedures.title: Investigate 'too many connections'
procedures.context: New connections fail with FATAL: sorry, too many clients already.
procedures.goal: Find the source of idle connections and free slots.

steps.command: SHOW max_connections;
steps.interpretation: The server allows 200 connections in total.

steps.command:
SELECT application_name, state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 3 DESC;
steps.interpretation: Many idle sessions from one app: missing pool or leak.

output_notes.anomaly: One app holding most slots: pool too big or leaking.

steps.command:
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle' AND state_change < now() - interval '1 hour';
steps.interpretation: Freed the long-idle sessions; fix the pool size to stop it recurring.

use_cases.title: App deploy doubled the pool
use_cases.situation: Each instance opens 50 connections; scaling out exhausted max_connections.

procedures.title: Create a read-only reporting user
procedures.context: The BI team needs read access to appdb without write privileges.
procedures.goal: Create the role, grant connect and read rights, including future tables.

steps.command: CREATE ROLE report LOGIN PASSWORD 'change-me';
steps.interpretation: Login role created.

steps.command: GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE appdb TO report;
steps.interpretation: Allowed to connect to appdb.

steps.command: GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO report;
steps.interpretation: Allowed to see objects in public.

steps.command: GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO report;
steps.interpretation: Can read every existing table.

steps.command: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO report;
steps.interpretation: Tables created later by the same owner are readable too.

use_cases.title: BI dashboards
use_cases.situation: A reporting tool needs read access without the risk of writes.

procedures.title: Check and reduce table bloat
procedures.context: The events table keeps growing although old rows are deleted daily.
procedures.goal: Confirm dead tuples and vacuum the table.

steps.command:
SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE relname = 'events';
steps.interpretation: Millions of dead rows and no autovacuum for a week.

steps.command: SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('events'));
steps.interpretation: Size before cleanup, for comparison.

steps.command: VACUUM (VERBOSE, ANALYZE) events;
steps.interpretation: Space becomes reusable inside the table; the file does not shrink without VACUUM FULL.
steps.output:
INFO:  finished vacuuming "appdb.public.events"
tuples: 9821004 removed, 2100400 remain
VACUUM

use_cases.title: Disk alert on the database volume
use_cases.situation: The events table grows daily although rows are deleted on schedule.
